subject: anatomy
title: Vertebral column and back: high-yield anatomy for NEET-PG and USMLE

steps.tx: The **vertebral column** has 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 coccygeal. Cervical vertebrae are identified by the **foramen transversarium**, which transmits the vertebral artery. Of the seven, C3 to C6 are typical, while C1, C2 and C7 are atypical. Exam questions often contrast typical cervical, thoracic and lumbar features, so learn the differences in shape of body, foramen, and facets.

steps.tx: A **hangman fracture** is a bilateral fracture through the pars interarticularis of C2, causing traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3. The canal is wide at this level, so cord injury is often absent. Check for vertebral artery injury and other cervical fractures. Anterior translation with C2-3 disc disruption signals instability. Imaging includes lateral and anteroposterior radiographs, CT, and MRI for disco-ligamentous injury.

steps.tx: The **lumbar puncture** needle passes through skin, subcutaneous fat, **supraspinous** and **interspinous ligaments**, then the **ligamentum flavum** and the epidural space before piercing dura and arachnoid. The usual site is L3-L4 or L4-L5 because the cord ends near L1-L2. The **iliac crest** highest point lies at the L3-L4 interval, a useful landmark. Muscles are not penetrated because they lie lateral to the midline.

steps.tx: **Disc prolapse** is most common at **L5-S1**, then L4-L5, and is rare at L3-L4 or above. The nucleus pulposus is white fibrocartilage, surrounded by the annulus fibrosus. The **erector spinae** group, made of iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis, extends the vertebral column when acting bilaterally and laterally flexes and rotates it when acting alone. Note that the lumbar region rotates least.
